title: Vijayadashami — Divine Shakti, Self-Knowledge, and Spiritual Practice
subtitle: Day 10

sections.title: Divine Feminine Energy and Self-Knowledge
content: Good morning, wonderful friends of Jnanodayam. During these nine days, we have been learning about Shakti, the Divine Mother's energy that pervades everything. Knowing about energy and directly knowing energy are different things. Knowing about Self-knowledge and actually knowing the Self are different. Knowing about truth and directly realizing truth are different. When we say “about,” we enter analysis, examination, and theory. What matters is practice. During the rainy season, conditions favor the growth of crops, and farmers know to sow their seeds then. Likewise, during Navaratri, the flow of energy is especially favorable. That is why Navaratri and Dasara are great festivals for meditators and spiritual practitioners.

All these observances exist for spiritual practice. We have now reached the tenth day, Vijayadashami, after the nine nights of Navaratri. What is the inner meaning of this festival? Without understanding its meaning, we merely perform ceremonies and rituals because our ancestors performed them. We should understand why we celebrate Vijayadashami. Every day we have been learning about Shakti and how to experience it directly. Yesterday we discussed seven principles. The first is that we receive energy through meditation.

There is energy throughout nature, and we receive it in other ways too. Listening to good music and uplifting sounds gives energy. Food also gives energy; that is its very purpose. We receive energy through the five senses. But meditation is the principal and most important means of receiving universal energy. As energy fills us and we become embodiments of energy, we begin to recognize consciousness. At first, energy and consciousness seem separate, but in truth they are one. They are never separate; they are two expressions of the same reality. Please understand this point carefully.

Energy and consciousness may appear different. When Kundalini Shakti rises upward and reaches consciousness, their oneness is realized. This is the principle of Ardhanarishvara: Mother Parvati and Shiva are not two but one. The knowledge born of their union is also one. Energy, consciousness, and the knowledge arising from their union—these three are experienced by every sincere meditator. Under the favorable conditions of Navaratri, we absorb abundant universal energy. Through energy we recognize consciousness, and through their union we gain knowledge. Our entire journey and practice are for Self-knowledge: Who am I? What should I do? What is my purpose? We must not misuse the energy awakened by our practice.

Universal energy, Kundalini energy, and the energy hidden within us must be used for great work. Hanuman used his strength in service of Rama's mission. We too need a grand purpose. This is the second principle. Our energy leaks away in many ways and is often misused. We must learn to contain it, as water is held in a reservoir, and then direct it toward our highest goal and its fulfillment.

The third point we discussed yesterday was that awakened energy takes two directions: inward and outward. When directed inward, we associate it with the feminine principle, feminine energy. When expressed in the external world, it manifests as masculine energy.

sections.title: Navaratri Practice and Inner Energy
content: Energy moves in these two directions. During the nine days of Navaratri, meditators remain more inwardly focused rather than outwardly engaged so that they may experience energy directly. Vijayadashami marks the beginning of victory: after storing energy within like a reservoir, we begin applying it in the outer world. We can observe both directions of energy. Within, energy can move upward or downward. The fourth point we discussed is that energy expressed outwardly helps us accomplish our work.

Whatever task we intend to complete, energy can help us bring it to fulfillment. The Pandavas, after their period of living incognito, retrieved the weapons they had hidden near the Shami tree, and from Vijayadashami onward they achieved victories they had not achieved before. There is a deeper meaning here. Energy activated through spiritual practice serves two purposes: accomplishment of work and attainment of knowledge. When it moves inward and upward, it leads to Self-knowledge and knowledge of Brahman. In the outer, material world, events, situations, and difficulties constantly arise, and we search for solutions.

We ask: Why is this happening? Why did this situation arise? When will this unbearable condition end? Why am I suffering? The root causes of external events must be sought within. What happens in the gross world also occurs in the subtle world. We must go still deeper, to the causal world, to discover the causes. This is why we speak of the causal body. It contains the design, plan, or pattern underlying events. If we keep searching only outside for the causes of what happens outside, we will never find them.

Everything has a relationship between cause and effect. According to this spiritual understanding, the causes of events in the outer world exist in the causal body and causal world. Only through meditation can we enter the great causal state and then go beyond causes, understanding them clearly. When both cause and effect are understood, a solution appears and the issue can be resolved. Albert Einstein is said to have observed that a problem cannot be solved at the same level of mind that created it. We must transcend the mind to find the solution. The Devi Mahatmyam offers a symbolic account of this. Lord Vishnu rests in yogic sleep.

The story says that Madhu and Kaitabha, two demons, arose from the wax of Vishnu's ears. These are symbols. Without understanding their inner meaning, we might laugh at the idea of demons emerging from earwax. Vishnu fought the two demons, who kept disturbing him, for five thousand years without defeating them. Five thousand years symbolically means a very long struggle. When he sought the help of Mahamaya, the Divine Mother and her Shakti, the demons were destroyed. The meaning is that we cannot conquer the mind by fighting it. Thinking is the mind's function. If we try to stop thoughts forcibly and declare war on the mind, we are the ones who lose.

The lesson of Vishnu's story is that we must go beyond the mind and draw upon divine energy rather than fight the mind. By awakening Shakti, we can rise to a state beyond it. Puranic stories contain profound meanings and knowledge; we should remember this whenever we read them. Events in the gross world have corresponding subtle patterns. The energetic or astral template, its design, and its root causes lie in the causal world and causal body.

Through meditation and the help of Shakti, we can reach the great causal state and go beyond cause and effect. We often discuss waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. We must transcend these three states and enter turiya. In that state, the bonds of cause and effect begin to fall away.

sections.title: Spiritual Stories and Their Inner Meanings
content: The sixth point concerns tamoguna and rajoguna. These qualities can obstruct the flow of energy and influence much of what happens within us. They should not dominate us. When tamas and rajas are excessive, we behave like the asuras. Sattva should predominate, leading us toward a pure sattvic state. Who has more energy? Those who meditate regularly and continuously. Their sattva increases. Laziness and negativity diminish; ego, possessiveness, attachment, and aversion gradually disappear. This is the inner battle against tamas and rajas symbolized by the slaying of Mahishasura during Navaratri.

These qualities act as blocks to energy. When energy flows strongly, it clears obstructions and redirects a flow that has gone astray. Consider a pipe blocked inside: a strong gush of water can clear the blockage. Similarly, we carry emotional and memory blocks—old fears, anger, sorrow, and many other emotions hardened within us. Intense practice, especially during favorable periods such as Navaratri, gradually clears them. This is the seventh point: purification of the network of nadis, the subtle energy channels. Obstacles are removed and the flow of energy finds a clear direction.
Vijayadashami has many inner meanings. We may also understand it as victory over the ten senses. When Shakti is awakened within, we gain greater control over our senses.

In North India, people burn an effigy of Ravana on Vijayadashami. Ravana's ten heads being destroyed symbolically reminds us to dissolve the ten-headed ego within ourselves. Ravana represents rajoguna and a level of development associated with the Manipura chakra. The battle between Rama and Ravana also carries an inner meaning. Some scriptures describe Rama himself undertaking spiritual practice before this great battle, because a great mission requires great energy and energy requires practice. Though Rama is understood as an incarnation of Vishnu, he lived in a human body and went through the human process of learning. He learned from Vishvamitra, who later directed him to the higher teacher Vasishta. Rama asked Vasishta many questions, expressing human emotions and sorrow, even asking why suffering exists and saying that he felt deeply depressed. Vasishta answered patiently. Their remarkable spiritual discussions are presented in thousands of verses. Before the war with Ravana, Rama too engaged in practice.

Great energy is needed to win a war. A great battle is also taking place within our minds, and we need energy to win it. These stories speak symbolically about that inner struggle. During Navaratri, Mahishasura's defeat represents victory over tamoguna. We should also remember the extraordinary episode of the Pandavas: they spent twelve years in the forest and one year living incognito. Why? We can understand that period too as a form of spiritual practice. The twelve years in the forest represent long, dedicated sadhana.

sections.title: The Importance of Practice in Life
content: Then came one year of ajnatavasa, living incognito. There is a profound meaning here. Forest life symbolizes silence, quietness, and meditative practice undertaken for a purpose. After twelve years of that practice, the Pandavas, although royal family members, had to live for a year without revealing their royal identity. They adopted disguises and ordinary roles.

Yudhishthira, also called Dharmaraja, became Kankabhatta, a companion and adviser in King Virata's court who played dice with the king. Bhima became the cook Vallabha. Arjuna became Brihannala, a dance teacher to Uttara, concealing his identity. Nakula cared for horses under another name.

Sahadeva, as Tantripala, tended cattle. Draupadi became Sairandhri, an attendant to Queen Sudeshna. Why did they do this? After twelve years of sadhana, subtle forms of ego can arise: “I have gained powers; I have acquired siddhis; whatever I wish happens.” Such ego becomes the first enemy of the spiritual seeker. Many practitioners become attached to extraordinary powers. The Pandavas' year of anonymity symbolizes conquering that ego.

During this period they did not misuse or display their strength. They kept it inwardly contained and concealed their weapons in a Shami or Jammi tree: Arjuna's Gandiva bow, Bhima's mace, arrows, and their other weapons. Weapons symbolize powers. A meditator should not display powers to impress others. Energy is not for personal glory; it is to be used at the right time for a great purpose. This is the deeper significance of honoring the Shami tree in India, a meaning we should not forget. Likewise, however great our outward identity may be—doctor, engineer, scientist, person of wealth or high position—we should set that identity aside. Bhima was not presenting himself as Bhima; he was a cook. Even one day of living without our usual identity could teach us something. We may not be able to live incognito for a whole year, but we can try setting aside the many masks and burdens of “I am this” or “I am that.” In the past, kings sometimes traveled in disguise, stayed among ordinary people, ate with them, and learned how they truly lived, because people often praised the king to his face and concealed their complaints. For meditators, the real lesson of ajnatavasa is to withdraw identification from the physical and social personality and remain grounded in spiritual identity. Indian festivals and epics carry extraordinary insights. While the Pandavas were at Virata's court, they faced many tests. Kichaka repeatedly humiliated Draupadi. Bhima and Dharmaraja felt anger, but they could not reveal their identities. Bhima could have killed him in a moment with one blow, yet they had to wait for the right time.

sections.title: Wisdom, Self-Reflection, and the Meaning of Victory
content: They observed and acknowledged their anger and other emotions with awareness. They did not merely suppress them; they waited for the right expression and the right time. They turned every failure into strength.

They transformed curses into blessings. An enlightened meditator turns every curse into a blessing; an unenlightened person may turn even a blessing into a curse. Through the vision of wisdom and a change in perception, a meditator can transform even an unbearable situation. For the Pandavas, twelve years in the forest and one year incognito were transformative. It was as if they had taken a second birth within the same lifetime: they became dvijas, twice-born, through self-realization and self-regeneration. On Vijayadashami, let us ask: What is our first victory? What is the very first success in our lives?

Please type your answer in the chat. Harika madam answered, “Being born.” Correct! Other things may be victories, but birth is the first victory. It began in the mother's womb. In this spiritual view, countless souls await an opportunity to incarnate; you were given the opportunity and chose your mother, father, and family as part of your divine plan. At the biological level, among countless sperm cells, only one fertilizes the ovum.

Of the countless souls, you received the opportunity to come to Earth. You faced the conditions of the womb and were born. Being born is your first victory, and it is also a great victory for your mother. Pregnancy might have ended in miscarriage, or the baby might not have survived after birth. But you arrived. The mother is an expression of Jagannmata, the Divine Mother, and has fulfilled the great role of bringing a divine soul into an earthly body. It is a victory for both mother and child. Now what is the final victory? Is it becoming a billionaire, gaining a position, or winning a Nobel Prize? Someone answered “conscious death.” Kings once thought conquering a kingdom was victory, but true victory is conquering ourselves. Knowing ourselves, attaining Atma Jnana and Brahma Jnana—these are the highest, ultimate successes. Our first victory begins with our mother; our final victory is fulfilled through the Divine Mother.

That final victory comes with the help of Jagannmata and Divine Shakti. On Vijayadashami, let us discuss a few principles. First is the principle of self-confidence. We often underestimate ourselves; that is great ignorance. The first step to victory is believing that the power of the Divine Mother herself lies within you. Many suffer from inferiority, fear, and a lack of complete faith in themselves. They believe others are great but do not see their own greatness. Everyone has greatness within. Some say, “I cannot meditate as well as others. They are wise masters, but I am not.” Yet we are all masters. Self-belief, self-confidence, self-worth, and self-esteem are the first steps. Many people undertake projects and work toward goals.

sections.title: Inner Transformation and Principles of Success
content: People undertake many tasks, but at the very beginning they think, “Perhaps I cannot do this; perhaps I do not have enough energy.” Once that feeling of inferiority is planted like a seed, it blocks the expression of their energy. We should begin every project with a noble and confident attitude. Second, victory is not about conquering the outer world but conquering the inner world. Along with our ten senses, the mind creates many obstacles: emotions, narrow thoughts, and ego. These are the real blocks.

During Navaratri, we symbolically destroy the inner Mahishasura and the other demons—Shumbha, Nishumbha, Dhumralochana, Raktabija, Madhu, Kaitabha, Vritrasura, and others. They are within us as negative qualities. How can we succeed in any project while these inner enemies dominate? Mahishasura symbolizes tamoguna, which expresses itself in many ways. Third, many people keep saying they will act in the future. But that imagined future never arrives. Every action and victory happens only in the present moment. We must succeed here and now. Leave the past behind on the riverbank. If we keep carrying old wounds, we cannot attain victory.

Anyone seeking genuine success must first win inwardly. When you win within, you can succeed outwardly and inspire many others to succeed. The nine days of Navaratri are dedicated to inner victory. Every spiritual discipline is a practice, and practice takes effort. A musician does not become accomplished in a single day; behind one beautiful song lie countless hours of practice. The same is true of an instrument, dance, sculpture, and meditation. Meditation requires sadhana.

Practice matters both inwardly and outwardly. Some say meditation needs no practice, that one can simply sit and meditate. But the mind pulls us in many directions. First we must train the body to sit and the eyes to remain closed. Eventually meditation becomes effortless, but until then practice is needed. Some observe Ayudha Puja on Navami and others on Vijayadashami. What does it mean? We thank the instruments and objects that help us—our vehicles, cars, bikes, and tools. We often take them to a temple and perform rituals, but we should understand their inner purpose.

We are expressing gratitude and tuning ourselves to these instruments, recognizing them as divine instruments useful in achieving our goals. Our greatest instruments are our body and mind. We must care for them and thank the body. We must use energy well, for accomplishment and for Atma Jnana and Brahma Jnana. Whatever we learn through meditation and practice, we should share with everyone. We seek Self-knowledge inwardly and teach what we have learned outwardly. Victory also rests on the principle of Karma Yoga: dedicated action and effort. On the physical plane, effort is necessary because there is a strong gravitational pull.

Next is the principle of gratitude. We must first thank and bow to our mother, because our first victory began with her. Behind our mother we honor Jagannmata, the Divine Mother who is the source of our energy. Then comes the principle of Aparajita, the undefeated one. Before retrieving their weapons from the Shami tree, the Pandavas connected with Goddess Aparajita and then took up their weapons.

sections.title: Self-Knowledge and a Vision for Life
content: Aparajita means the power that is undefeated, the state of no defeat. The Pandavas held that feeling of “no failure.” On Vijayadashami, remember that our first success came through our mother, while our ultimate success comes through knowing ourselves. We discover our energy and gain the wisdom arising from the union of energy and consciousness. Conscious death and other attainments are fruits of how we live. Those who become masters of their inner world and gain wisdom through direct experience live wonderfully in the outer world as well.

Whatever we undertake on Vijayadashami, let us begin with a strong connection to the infinite energy present within ourselves and everyone. We should act with the conviction that we can use that energy to accomplish our task. The beginning matters most. The first step leads to a thousand steps, yet we hesitate at the first step, asking, “Can I climb? Can I do it? Will it work?” Today we should recognize and remove self-doubt.

Wonderful friends, we have observed Navaratri beautifully and entered energetic states. But practice does not end today. We were more attentive during these favorable days; afterward we should still meditate for an hour every day. Our sadhana must be continuous, both inwardly and outwardly. Inward practice is meditation; outward practice is the way we live, the situations we face, and the people with whom we interact. Everything in life can become sadhana. Today let us do a small exercise concerning real success. To succeed, we must not doubt whether our goal will be attained. If our goal is Self-knowledge, it brings inner bliss and peace and benefits our outer life as well.

We must remove self-doubt and become inwardly what we wish to attain. Imagine the feeling you would have if your project or goal were already accomplished, and feel that feeling now. Whatever your profession, see yourself as successful in it. That future possibility already exists subtly within you like a seed. The doubting mind—the “Doubting Thomas” mind—keeps blocking it.

Thoughts such as “It may be difficult,” “I may fail,” and “I will do it later” hold us back. Such negativity and postponement are expressions of tamoguna. We should experience our highest possibility right now, in this present moment, as if we had already become it. For example, you may be like a drop of water, while your highest possibility is the vast ocean. That possibility exists within you; someday you will realize it.
Even while you are a tiny drop, feel yourself to be the ocean now. The entire ocean is hidden within the drop.

sections.title: Transformation Through Practice
content: Suppose you currently teach meditation to one hundred people a day, but your goal in this lifetime is to teach ten million people. Through meditation, they may experience inner transformation, joy, and wisdom. Is teaching ten million people possible? That future already exists in subtle seed form as a possibility. Feel it now. See yourself on the day when your goal has been fulfilled.

Imagine that you have taught meditation to ten million people, inspired them toward a vegetarian way of life, and helped organize ten million meditation yajnas. Imagine these great achievements and connect now with your highest possibility. Friends, let us close our eyes for a short four-minute process on this auspicious Vijayadashami. Let us attune ourselves to the victory we wish to attain. Connect with the breath, observe inhalation and exhalation, and quiet the mind. Remember that our mother gave us our first victory by bringing us into this world. Our relationship with our mother is our first successful relationship. Let us thank her.

Recognize our mother as the source of that first victory. Feel gratitude fully. Now picture yourself in the future, having accomplished a meaningful goal. It may be Self-knowledge, a project, a talent, or an expression of creativity. Feel now what your future self would feel on achieving that success.

In your subtle inner world, visualize yourself fully developed, with your full potential awakened, victorious inwardly and outwardly. Experience now the feeling of that future day. Observe your future self, and allow that future self and your present self to become one in this moment.

Set aside self-doubt and feelings such as “I am worthless,” “I am unworthy,” “I am inadequate,” and “I am not good enough.” Put aside doubts about whether the goal will happen. Tune fully into the experience of success. Some feel joy; others feel peace, completeness, fulfillment, or the sense that life has become meaningful. Whatever that feeling is, experience it now in your body. Breathe gently and remain in it for a minute. “I am victorious; there is no defeat for me.” Slowly open your eyes with a peaceful smile.

There is only success, no failure. From today, let us erase the word “failure” from our dictionary. One success leads to another, and then another, both inwardly and outwardly. Take your time opening your eyes, dear friends. May you be victorious; may you achieve great victory. Blessings to you all. Wonderful friends, let us now celebrate Vijayadashami by listening to a beautiful song from Harika madam.

sections.title: Self-Awareness and Participant Reflections
content: [A chanting-only performance of the Durga Sukta by Harika is omitted.] Wonderful, Harika madam. You offered everyone such a beautiful chant for Vijayadashami. Thank you. Let us now hear from participants, including some who have been waiting since yesterday and some who are new. First is Sandhya, whose birthday is today.

Sandhya: Namaste, sir. Through these Jnanodayam classes you are giving us so much wisdom. Earlier I kept struggling, thinking, “I do not have this or that,” and searching for reasons. Now I do not even feel the need to ask those questions. Everything is there. Through practice, we must search inwardly. I was searching outside for causes and could not find them; today you explained that we should look within. The Mother's energy is infinite. When I was not connected with her, I behaved as though I knew everything and made mistakes without understanding. Today I ask her forgiveness. I seek your blessings so that this wisdom becomes firmly established within me. You have said in earlier classes that Ganesha is at Muladhara, that Mother and Father are within us, that Shanmukha is within us, that Sita is at Muladhara and Rama at Sahasrara, and that we must hold on to the breath, Hanuman. I did not understand how precious the breath was and kept running here and there. Now I am learning to sit. I feel good simply sitting; I no longer feel like going anywhere. I wish to begin this inward journey, and I ask for your blessings.

Teacher: Wonderful, Sandhya madam. Happy birthday. Thank you to your parents. I wish you wonderful spiritual growth and the attainment of great states of the Self through meditation. Thank you also for making a donation to Quantum Life University programs on your birthday.

Ashwini and Narasimha: Namaste, sir. Happy Dasara. From these nine days of classes I have learned a great deal. I am listening to the classes and attending workshops. When you explained the subtle qualities within us, I began observing them during meditation over the last four days. After the Eckhart Tolle book series, I have been reading the book again and putting it into practice. I practice not only in meditation but in ordinary daily life. I notice that I still think about the past; such thoughts arise without my knowing. I am applying what I learned even outside my regular meditation. Thank you.

Teacher: Wonderful. Thank you for sharing. A question from Sushmita in the YouTube chat asks: What is Vipassana meditation? How is it different from Anapanasati, and which is better? They are not two competing things. The starting point is always Anapanasati, awareness of the breath. Through that practice, the state or experience of Vipassana arises. Buddha first taught everyone to begin with Anapanasati.

sections.title: Dasara Message and Questions and Answers
content: The Buddha explained how to observe inhalation and exhalation. Then come states described as kayanupassana, vedananupassana, cittanupassana, and dhammanupassana. These are experiences and stages of observation. Vipassana is seeing in a special, clear way—seeing truth as truth and falsehood as falsehood. Beyond that lies the state of nirvana. These are logical, sequential steps, one after another. Do not be confused: meditation begins with awareness of inhalation and exhalation. Vipassana is a fruit of that practice. Through practice, many experiences, including those associated with the third eye, may arise.

The host invites Usha Sayani to speak, but she initially has difficulty unmuting. The host asks her to accept the request or click the blue unmute button and says they will return to her. Meanwhile, Mitra Ramadevi is invited to share.

Ramadevi: Namaste, sir. My heartfelt salutations to Patriji, Patriji madam, you, Lakshmi madam, and the QLU community. Happy Dasara to everyone. I have been meditating every day during Navaratri. Your classes have been wonderful. We meditate from 9 p.m. to 5 a.m. at night and another two hours at the center in the afternoon—ten hours a day. We hardly sleep, yet we feel healthy and active and continue our work. We hold meditation sessions at a different person's house each day. In meditation, I experience myself as a complete soul, connected with the Divine Mother, like a little child in her lap. Today, while meditating in a room, I saw a large tiger sitting in front of me. Someone came and asked how I could sit in a room with a tiger. I replied that I had been sitting there looking at it for three hours.

I feel great joy. This Navaratri meditation has been extraordinary, and I am learning much wisdom from your classes. I now believe I will achieve my goal: to establish a meditation center with a pyramid where thousands or lakhs of people can sit, meditate, gain wisdom, receive the nectar of meditation, and leave healthy and happy. I have the firm confidence that I will complete this goal in this lifetime. I feel that through practice what I intend can happen. Thank you for giving me this opportunity.
Teacher: Thank you, Ramadevi madam. You described your experiences beautifully.

Usha: Namaste, sir. Dasara greetings to you, Lakshmi madam, Harika madam, and everyone here. I am very happy today. In these nine days, I learned that the many qualities represented by the demons exist within us and how to remove them. Earlier I knew only that the Goddess killed demons; I did not understand their inner meaning. I have experienced some transformation. When difficulties arose at home, I learned to accept them and work through them. From the tenth through the thirty-first, we have organized twenty-one days of twelve-hour meditation sessions, held in different homes. We are all participating, experiencing the energy and putting into practice what you teach each morning. I feel the Divine Mother is giving me the strength to practice this wisdom. I am deeply grateful. Please visit the Trimurti Pyramid Meditation Center at Meerpet; we invite you. Thank you.
Teacher: Wonderful. Your continuous meditation program is excellent.

Venkateswarulu: Namaste, sir. Happy Vijayadashami to everyone in the group and to your family. I received so much knowledge through these nine days. I understood that everything is in Mother Earth and the Divine Mother and that we should connect with her. I spent more time meditating this year. Though I am far away, I feel fortunate to receive this wisdom through you. My wife also meditates, and meditation is a part of our daily life. Jnanodayam has been very useful in my life. Thank you for allowing me to speak.
Teacher: Thank you, Venkateswarulu. Wonderful. Next, Venkata Lakshmi Devi; let us all keep our sharing brief.

sections.title: Putting Spiritual Wisdom into Practice
content: Venkata Lakshmi Devi: Namaste, sir, and greetings to all masters. Happy Vijayadashami. We listen to your classes every day; they are wonderful. I have had trouble using Zoom, but I want to share an experience from yesterday. For four days I felt that the Goddess was calling me to visit her temple. I was meditating at home. About fifteen days earlier, during meditation, I had experienced going to Nagaloka, the realm of serpents, and another golden realm. My mind told me not to go to the temple because it was hot and I could go tomorrow. Then I became more aware and recognized that my mind was distracting me. I felt the Mother might be calling me to tell me something, so I went.

When I arrived at the Kanyaka Parameswari temple, I was astonished. It was decorated to resemble Nagaloka, with serpents, anthills, and scenes very similar to what I had seen in meditation. I was amazed and even a little afraid when I remembered how large the serpents had appeared. If I had lost awareness and stayed home, I would not have seen this. I meditated there. People offered their homes for me to conduct classes. I felt as though Hanuman and the Divine Mother were encouraging me to teach. These experiences feel miraculous to me. Quantum Life University offers extraordinary wisdom. You teach what the rishis and yogis practiced and ask us to practice it too. The Durga hymn chanted today was powerful. We had become hesitant about temple worship and Sanskrit chants, but through your teaching we have begun visiting temples, practicing at home, and learning Sanskrit hymns and Vedic teachings again. I am grateful to you, Lakshmi madam, Harika madam, all the masters, and especially the Divine Mother. The Divine Mother and Ardhanarishvara are within us. We need not run outside; we must undertake the inward journey. I have been reading the book Antaryanam since the festival began and enjoy its explanation of breath and the stages of inner travel. I am happy to be your student and to have come to this university. Finding a great teacher who guides us on the right path is my real Vijayadashami.
Teacher: Wonderful, Venkata Lakshmi Devi madam. Thank you very much.

Vijaya: Namaste, sir. Gratitude to you and Lakshmi madam for giving us this wisdom. Earlier I thought these stories were simply stories, but now I understand their subtle meanings. I have recognized and worked on some of the qualities within me. I used to doubt whether I could teach meditation and get people to sit and practice. Today I felt as though people had already come, learned meditation, and that I had taught them. I used to perform worship for nine days every year. This time, when an accident caused an injury to my leg, I understood through meditation that the Mother had protected me from something worse. I felt grateful. Thank you for all the wisdom.

Teacher: Wonderful, Vijaya madam. Happy Vijayadashami. It is amazing that you gained inner courage. Thank you to the entire QLU community, especially Harika, under whose leadership Jnanodayam began, and to Surya, Charan, Anjan, and the other team members.
Host: I would like to introduce our new team member, Divya, who has been helping us for the last ten days.

Divya: Namaste, and happy Dasara to everybody. It is wonderful to be part of the QLU back-end team. QLU is a reason I am here today. There are many people like me who do not yet know why they are here or what their purpose is. I want this wisdom to reach them too. I truly wish for initiatives such as Dhyana Jagat to succeed.

Teacher: Wonderful, Divya. You have been supporting and coordinating things behind the scenes. Jnanodayam is great teamwork, and I appreciate all team members. Is Latha Mahendra madam here? I think she has left; she joins every day. No problem. We will meet again. Thank you, dear friends, and Vijayadashami greetings once again to you and your families.

sections.title: Closing Message
content: Thank you, sir. On behalf of everyone whose voices we cannot hear individually today, I am thanking you. You gave us your time for ten days and shared unlimited wisdom with us. [The supplied Telugu transcript ends mid-sentence.]
